title: How does a film explore its mystery without losing the intrigue?

commenti.body: Kill List is a perfect example of a mystery/thriller that never gives itself up.  Even when the hand is revealed, the viewer can’t be certain what just happened. I have never seen a film filled with as much dread in my life while being completely floored by the slow reveal of the mystery. Masterful work from Ben Wheatley.

> when there was a certain mysticism to the events in the film. But as the film tries to explain itself, I can't help but compare the film to real world logic

Because in a blind scenario, you don't know where a story is gonna go since it could go anywhere. You don't know the rules, the stakes, the threshold, nor what the film is capable of. Once a story starts to develop and explain itself, however, it simultaneously cuts off all other possibilities that could logically follow. The more that is revealed the more inversely predictable a story becomes.

But I'd argue that's actually a good problem and a story without an explanation, or at least too vague an explanation, feels like the writer is hiding his lack of ideas behind a thin pretense of vagueness. The best way to handle this issue is to not have your story hinge on the mystery in and of itself but rather escalate other elements while slowly deescalating the mystery.

I love Korean film, so I’ll use two examples from that lens:

*Memories of Murder* is an example of an amazing thriller largely because it balances out characters’ certainty over who the killer is with a nagging, unrelenting ambiguity and doubt within the objective reality of the mystery. The corrupt detectives each have their own certainty as to how to solve the case, but the universe refuses to bend to their will.

*Burning* is a slow burn thriller that achieves a similar sense of mystique due to a quiet but intense subjectivity on part of the main character. As he becomes more and more obsessed over the mystery, and more and more convinced that Steven Yeun’s character is to blame, we as the viewer become more and more pigeonholed into the main character’s subjective experience, clouding the truth to the point where we can’t be certain by the end what is reality and what is in the character’s fantasy.

You might like 1975's PICNIC AT HANGING ROCK. It's part of the unofficial film genre that is deliberately ambiguous, that withholds definitive answers about what happened or what is real. Most folks find such films unsatisfying, but it seems to be quite your cup of tea!

> Masterful work from Ben Wheatley.

Ben and his wife and frequent collaborator Amy Jump are two to keep a close eye on.

I didn't *love* Kill List.  I liked it a lot, but his later stuff was better.

"A Field in England" is a REALLY hard sell if you got a buddy over and they want to watch a movie, but it's so damned good.  High Rise is similar.

I should probably re-watch Kill List because I was kinda cinema-illiterate the first time around and didn't think much about it, but I know Wheatley and Jump are nothing but net otherwise.

It's the same thing as a twist ending. You should be able to slap your forehead and say "so *that's* why it did that!". A random collection of scenes should come together and reveal the theme of the story.

I think this is why "the monster represents mental illness" is such a common trope recently.

Escalating other elements while deescalating the mystery is a great way to put it! While maybe not the perfect example, Blow Out comes to mind. The layers of the mystery are peeled back while the depth of the protagonist's obsession and stakes of their involvement in the conspiracy escalate and sort of take over the role the mystery was once taking.

One way I'd describe this is about trading off different sources of intrigue. In a well designed story when we learn the solution to one question its answer should immediate raise new questions. Usually the arc of this is moving from plot mysteries to character/thematic questions, though more genre fare might trade off a series of plot questions that have raising tension. A simple case would be something like revealing the identity of the killer at the same time as introducing his final plan that needs to be stopped. I recently watched *Manhunter* which generally does a good job with this. Either pairing each revelation with a new question to maintain plot momentum or with intensifying questions about how this is affecting Will Graham's psychological state. 

I agree with your feelings on *Cure*. I think some of the issue is that the questions it was dealing with were more specific to Japan in the 80s and 90s. Ideas around disconnection from society were big in a post bubble era. A number of high profile murder cases in that period lead to a lot of art around questions of what leads various sorts of people to murder. Apocalyptic sorts of cults were also in conversation. Remember that the original title was *Evangelist* before the subway sarin gas attacks. I think the question of whether the killer would start a serious movement was intended from the ending in a way that doesn't come across as strongly now. Compare, say, [Suicide Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_Club_(film\)).

That being said, I also think its later questions simply strain belief in a way that hurts it. One important thing for supernatural works is to establish reasonably well which ideas are intended literally and which figuratively. If you're asking the audience to make major departures from their version of reality then questions about how that alternate world would be simply aren't as interesting as ones about our own reality. There needs to be some mapping back to consensus reality. You can imagine an alternate version where they play up the mesmerism stuff less and leave it as some preternatural charisma. Then it could leave current viewers with ideas about current fixations like radicalization and "lone wolf" terrorists.
But since it committed to something specific and fake my final idea was "it sure would suck if mind control magic was real".

For me personally, a great mystery film should raise questions that cannot just be answered by "the butler was the killer" (unless of course it's just trying to be a light entertainment) 

It should make the viewer ponder on endless questions of above all human nature, greed, obsession, jealousy, faith, power. Klute, The Conversation, Night Moves and The Pledge are all great at this.

The perfect example would be The Vanishing. If you were to explain to someone the "mystery", it would come across as absurdly common and straightforward. But the way its presented forces the viewer to feel very emotionally and intellectually engaged even after multiple viewings.

Can say I definitely had the same experience with the cure. 


I dont watch that much horror-mystery but I would think the problem you are describing is really a problem of that genre, I dont know if there is really a solution to it. I would be tempted to call those movies "fake" in a way. They draw us in by presenting us with a mystery that is aching to get resolved, but then there is nothing to really get resolved as there wasnt any serious substance beneath it.



I think the succesful films have some substance beneath the mystery and then the movement is that the film shifts from mysterious to actually resolving the plotline, character conflicts, themes, etc...


I think a good example would be Villeneuves Arrival. At first its just "Oooh Aliens, mysterious, what are they doing?" but then as the plot unravels there emerges both a gripping conflict as Amy Addams tries to fight for peace against those anxious, triggerhappy military operatives, as well as an unveiling of interesting philosophical themes around eternal recurrence and whatnot.


I cant think of a good example right now but I think in the classical horror-mystery genre a succesful payoff would be if the monster or ghost haunting your mansion actually has some interesting family drama background or origin story. Then all the vague hints in the mysterious beginning come together to form a complete picture and then the final arc is about somehow resolving that drama.

Then all the vague hints in the mysterious beginning come together to form a complete picture and then the final arc is about somehow resolving that drama, by idk racing to get to the monsters grandpa and finding the trinket or whatever.


This seems like a clicheed example, and it is to a degree, but I still think thats roughly the formula how to have the mystery movie actually end with a satisfying payoff/final arc. To make a really good movie, its then in the details, if its e.g. an actually interesting and monster origin story that somehow resonates with the human condition in a deeper way, or just how good the scenes are as the movie shifts towards the action or thriller genre.
Another great highlight of the Aussie New Wave.

Some films are more about atmosphere than story. In those cases, explaining the mystery tends to deflate the armor.

I think this is well illustrated by comparing blir classics. I know *The Maltese Falcon* is extremely highly regarded, and I partly agree, but for me it kind of deflates in the last third or so when everything is explained. In contrast, *The Big Sleep* retains its mysterious atmosphere throughout (partly because even the writers didn't know what actually happened in the story), and I think it's the superior film for it.

I feel as though the film's explanation was the only place for the film to go, and even in its third act it still retains the mystery it established in the first two acts. When Sakuma explains soul conjuring to Takabe and we are shown the scene where Sakuma is standing in front of the asylum with the Japanese professor in the window, the mystery is still there. When Takabe is on the bus with his wife in the clouds, the mystery is still there. When Takabe is listening to the Japanese professor's world via phonograph, the mystery is still there. 

 There is an element of mystery and intrigue in Cure, but its entirely possible that you weren't satisfied with what the film gave you. I think when people try to apply logic to certain mysterious films, its the films that don't hold up because the people are trying to force real world logic on films that don't need it.
>Burning is a masterpiece, I strongly recommend it to anyone reading this

A good mystery drop feeds clues at the right time so you can piece stuff together but never enough to let you solve it until the big reveal.

As for mystery in horror, I don't think it really works, the fun part about mystery is the logical process of solving it while solving the mystery in horror annihilates the tension. My favorite horror films end leaving you with more questions than answers.

Most of my favorite movies are ambiguous throughout. I find it funny that many of the comments here are explaining how you shouldn't want an ambiguous movie?? Creating a specific atmosphere and mood is much more engaging to me than a solid story or character development. And of course BOTH can exist, but when a story is neatly tied up I usually don't think about it much afterwards, where an ambiguous movie will stay in my head for weeks. It's just more fun to think about.

Ive thought a lot about this, and I think it has to do with plot and themes of a film running parallel, and occasionally intersecting, with the character philosophy and what is happening in their world, but ultimately they are never on the same train tracks, so we never get all the pieces.

For instance, I would argue that half the reason that Seven works is that there is never a full explanation about John Doe. We see a plot trying to follow him and picking up the pieces of his brutal crimes, gli.paes of what makes him tick, and the exploration of other life philosophies to the same world though Somerset, Mills, and Tracy. We can ultimately see what John Doe is getting at, but we never get a satisfying answer. The more you watch the film, more you pick up, but the further the understanding is.

>especially in the mystery horror/thriller genre

Well, if I stick to that, most of what I discuss below will be irrelevant to your post.  I widen out the discussion a little

By "mystery" I parse you actually mean "puzzle."

A mystery and a puzzle are not the same thing.

You give that away with "Having explanations to the mystery [...]."

Murder mysteries are typically puzzles.  I can accept the use of "mystery" to label that genre, so much of my comment might seem nitpicking.

But how paltry and silly a murder mystery seems next to an actual mystery--a Mystery--outside of fiction, such as the Mystery of existence, or the Mystery of Time; or the Mystery of Transubstantiation, or the Mystery of the Incarnation in Christianity; or the Mystery of the Sephiroth in the kabbalah; or the Mystery of "atman is Brahman" in Hinduism; and so on.  But you seem to want puzzles.

One can explore a Mystery--that's one aspect of a Mystery, to engage a mind; typically, one does not and cannot explore a puzzle.  One attempts to solve a puzzle.  That's all.  And such solutions are typically intellectual or rational.  But one cannot solve a Mystery.  The encounter of a Mystery is typically non-intellectional and non-rational.  It is on a different plane of experience altogether.  But you seem to want an intellectual and rational approach.

I know some movies do offer Mystery.  But I suspect those are the kinds of movies you would not like.

Further, I suspect by "ambiguous" you mean something else, such as "Not immediately explained or understood or solved."  But that is not what ambiguity means to me.  I could point out and perhaps even discuss this aspect or that aspect of something I consider ambiguous, but I do not solve an ambiguity; I do not understand an ambiguity.  But you seem to want understanding.

Indeed, in art, there is no reason whatsoever to try to solve or understand an ambiguity.  Typically, an artist presents an ambiguity so that a viewer can contemplate it *as* an ambiguity, as something of value in and of itself.  But you seem to want explanations and don't actually like ambiguity.

There are common emotions, such as feeling happy (as when watching a comedy) or feeling sad (as when watching a drama).  And many people assert or imply those kinds of emotions, and similar common ones, are the ones which matter.  They want a movie to give them that, and any movie which doesn't, they complain about.  They want what they want.  Like you.  You seem to want these common emotions.

There are uncommon emotions too, emotions few movies depict characters feeling or invite a viewer to feel, such as the experience of the sublime, or being overwhelmed, and so on.  And an encounter with those things is not a substitute for something else; a movie which offers these uncommon emotions is not (necessarily) defective.  A movie which does not solve its Mysteries for viewers is not wrong.  In a certain frame of mind, experiencing an ambiguity may lead a viewer to experience an amazing uncommon emotion, and thus realize something about himself in addition to realizing something about the ambiguity.  (In effect, as I explore an ambiguity, the ambiguity allows me to explore myself.)  But that realization is not a common emotion.  And you are clear you don't want that.

No spoilers, but it's maybe the perfect example of a film relevant to the points you made in the OP.

Not the OP but I watched it a while ago but rated it highly. I am aware that the disappearance wasn't concluded properly (a soft explanation exists floating around, but it's an awful one) but my rating hinged more on that the film stands strong in spite of not having an explanation. For me, the lack of explanation was less of a manipulative/cowardly choice but more of stylistically Lovecraftian/slice-of-life choice in the sense that some things in life are just never explained. So it didn't bother me as much because 1) the rest of the film was still good and 2) the lack of explanation felt like a stylistic choice rather than a way to protect someone's ego or poor writing. The same with Bong Joon-ho's "Memories of Murder," which also ended without an explanation on purpose but not in a manipulatively, intellectually condescending way.

Have you ever seen *Last Year at Marienbad*? That's another classic film that divides viewers because of its ambiguity.

In the [words](https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/last-year-at-marienbad/) of critic Eric Henderson:

>The recurring attitude throughout most interpretations of *Marienbad*—both positive and negative—is that of sheer interpretation fatigue. While some could likely take that as a sign of exasperation, it’s also a testament to the movie’s uncanny, hypnotic power over those willing to submit to its complex mélange of non-clues.
